title: A Nationwide Study on the Impact of Routine Testing for EGFR Mutations in Advanced NSCLC Reveals Distinct Survival Patterns Based on EGFR Mutation Subclasses.
abstract: EGFR mutation analysis in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients is currently standard-of-care.

We determined the uptake of EGFR testing, test results and survival of EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients in the Netherlands, with the overall objective to characterize the landscape of clinically actionable EGFR mutations and determine the role and clinical relevance of uncommon and composite EGFR mutations.
Non-squamous NSCLC patients diagnosed in 2013, 2015 and 2017 were identified in the Netherlands Cancer Registry (NCR) and matched to the Dutch Pathology Registry (PALGA).
Between 2013-2017, the uptake of EGFR testing gradually increased from 72.7% to 80.9% (p p EGFR mutations (n = 925; 11.7%; 95% confidence interval (CI), 11.0-12.4) nor the distribution of variants.
For patients treated with first-line EGFR inhibitors (n = 651), exon 19 deletions were associated with longer OS than L858R (HR 1.58; 95% CI, 1.30-1.92; p p p = 0.069).

Our analysis indicates that grouping exon 19 deletions and L858R into one class of 'common' EGFR mutations in a clinical trial may mask the true activity of an EGFR inhibitor towards specific mutations.

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the leading cause of global cancer-related deaths [].

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: Activating mutations in EGFR account for the second most common mechanism of malignant transformation in NSCLC in western Europe and the United States [].

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: Clinical trials have demonstrated that first-line treatment with an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), such as gefitinib [], erlotinib [], afatinib [], dacomitinib [], or osimertinib []. improves survival of advanced NSCLC patients with EGFR exon 19 deletions and L858R point mutations.

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: Therefore, molecular diagnostics to detect these and other EGFR mutations has been standard-of-care in Europe since 2010 [,,].

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: Molecular testing has since evolved from a single-gene polymerase chain reaction-based approach to the implementation of multiplex analyses such as next-generation sequencing (NGS) in routine diagnostics for the detection of multiple gene variants in a limited amount of tissue [,].

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: A multiplex analysis is particularly useful for NSCLC due to often limited amount of available tissue and the increasing number of predictive markers beyond EGFR (including BRAF, ERBB2 and MET) [,,].

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: The Dutch National Healthcare Institute does not specify the methodology or commercially available companion diagnostic test that must be used for the evaluation of these biomarkers.

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: Instead, individual molecular laboratories perform local validation of sequencing techniques according to national accreditation guidelines (ISO-NEN-15189:2012 since 2016/2017) [].

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: All NGS panels used in the Netherlands cover the full region of interest in EGFR (exons 18-21).

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: There have been limited evaluations of the real-world, population-level effect of changes in routine EGFR testing and the introduction of multiplex testing on the landscape of EGFR mutations and overall survival rates.

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: Furthermore, the clinical relevance of uncommon and composite EGFR mutations remains elusive.

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: In the Netherlands, all patients diagnosed with cancer are registered in the Netherlands Cancer Registry (NCR), managed by the Netherlands Comprehensive Cancer Organization (IKNL).

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: In addition, the nationwide network and registry of histo- and cytopathology in the Netherlands (PALGA) maintains a database of all pathology reports from pathology departments in the Netherlands [].

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: The effects of routine EGFR mutation testing for advanced NSCLC patients on a population-level scale in 2013, 2015 and 2017 were evaluated following a query of both registries.

body.section: 1. Introduction
body.text: During this period, only gefitinib, erlotinib and afatinib were available for use in first-line treatment.

body.section: 2.1. Patient Selection
body.text: Testing for EGFR mutations has been standard-of-care in the Netherlands since 2011 [], and NGS has gradually been implemented into the routine setting for non-squamous NSCLC (ns-NSCLC).

body.section: 2.1. Patient Selection
body.text: Therefore, data were requested from the NCR and PALGA for advanced NSCLC patients diagnosed in 2013, 2015 and 2017.

body.section: 2.1. Patient Selection
body.text: All patients recorded in the NCR who were diagnosed with advanced adenocarcinoma of the lung, adenosquamous carcinoma of the lung and NSCLC not otherwise specified (NOS) were included.

body.section: 2.1. Patient Selection
body.text: Patients were matched with the nationwide PALGA registry to retrieve the pathology reports.

body.section: 2.1. Patient Selection
body.text: Data requests were approved by the scientific and privacy committees of IKNL (application numbers K15.115, K16.264, and K18.311) and PALGA (application numbers LZV1172, LZV2016-91, LZV2018-199).

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: Variables retrieved from the NCR included sex, age at diagnosis, morphology code (ICD-O 3rd edition), type of first-line treatment (categories including chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery, targeted therapy, other therapy, a combination of these, or no therapy), overall survival (OS) (time in days from diagnosis to death or data cut-off) and vital status as of 1 February 2020.

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: Molecular testing results were manually extracted from the pathology reports by dedicated researchers (CCHJK, BNCG, BK).

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: Extracted variables included whether testing was performed or not, the type of molecular test(s) used to detect EGFR mutations, an identifier of the pathology department that requested the test, and the reported EGFR mutation status.

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: The type of molecular test(s) used were corrected to exclude secondary testing on new tissue obtained at progressive disease.

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: Reported EGFR driver mutations were reannotated in accordance with the Human Genome Variant Society recommendations for the description of sequence variants [].

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: Each variant was classified for predicted actionability with EGFR-TKI as ‘sensitive’ or ‘no benefit’, with level of evidence tiers based on the 2017 Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP)/American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO)/College of American Pathologists (AMP) guidelines [].

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: Patients with EGFR mutations were grouped into one of five nominal categories based on the frequency of the reported EGFR mutations and the AMP/ASCO/CAP level of evidence (Figure 1).

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: These categories included: exon 19 deletion (sensitive, Tier IA); L858R (sensitive, Tier IA); uncommon, actionable (sensitive, Tier IB/IIC/IID); exon 20 insertion (no benefit expected, Tier IIC) or not actionable/unknown (no benefit expected, Tier I-IV, except for exon 20 insertions).

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: In case of a double variant, actionability was assessed for the combination.

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: For example, the combination of uncommon, actionable variants E709A and G719A has been reported to be sensitive to afatinib [], and the combination is thus tiered IIC (uncommon, actionable).

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: However, if evidence for the combination was lacking, the patient was assigned according to the highest Tier of the individual variants.

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: For instance, patients with a combination of an exon 19 deletion (Tier IA) and a variant of unknown significance (Tier III) were assigned to category ‘exon 19 deletion’.

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: Classification was performed by a certified clinical scientist in molecular pathology (LCvK) [], and only considered for first- and second-generation EGFR-TKI (gefitinib, erlotinib, afatinib) due to the unavailability of first-line osimertinib treatment in the study period.

body.section: 2.2. Data Extraction and Handling
body.text: Clinical data processing was performed in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679.

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: Statistical analysis was performed with SPSS version 23 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA).

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: Comparisons were performed for patient characteristics, testing rates and EGFR mutation detection rates between the three years of diagnosis (2013, 2015 and 2017) and between testing modalities (multi-gene assays or single-gene tests).

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: Multi-gene assays were defined as NGS technologies or massARRAY.

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: Proportional differences between years were assessed using Pearson’s Chi-square analysis, and, if significant, a subgroup analysis was performed with Fisher’s exact tests.

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: Differences between testing modalities were assessed using Fisher’s exact tests.

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: Median OS from date of diagnosis was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method, including 95% confidence intervals (CI), and tested for significance with the Log-rank test.

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: For EGFR-mutant patients treated with first-line targeted therapy, uni- and multivariate Cox regression analyses were performed to correct for the co-variables age, sex, year of diagnosis and tumor histology.

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: Variables with a p-value < 0.05 in the univariate analysis were included in the multivariate analysis (forward stepwise logistic regression).

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: Hazard ratio (HR) and 95% CI were calculated.

body.section: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
body.text: Differences were considered statistically significant at a p-value < 0.05.

body.section: 3.1. Patients Included in the Analysis
body.text: The NCR recorded 3393, 3712 and 3746 advanced ns-NSCLC patients in 2013, 2015 and 2017, respectively.

body.section: 3.1. Patients Included in the Analysis
body.text: Of these, 3195 (2013), 3423 (2015) and 3636 (2017) could be matched to excerpts in the PALGA registry, creating a population-level cohort of 10,254 Dutch advanced ns-NSCLC patients (Figure 2).

body.section: 3.1. Patients Included in the Analysis
body.text: Patient characteristics are shown in Table 1.

body.section: 3.1. Patients Included in the Analysis
body.text: The mean age for the total population was 66.9 years.

body.section: 3.1. Patients Included in the Analysis
body.text: A small majority of patients was male (53.6%).

body.section: 3.1. Patients Included in the Analysis
body.text: The majority of patients were diagnosed with adenocarcinoma (86.3%), followed by NSCLC-not otherwise specified (NSCLC-NOS) (13.1%), and adenosquamous carcinoma (0.6%).

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: Out of the total population of 10,254 advanced NSCLC patients, 77.1% (95% CI, 76.3-77.9%; n = 7908) were tested for EGFR mutations.

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: The testing rate increased significantly throughout the study period, from 72.7% (95% CI, 71.2-74.2%) in 2013 to 77.2% (95% CI, 75.8-78.6%) in 2015 (p < 0.001), up to 80.9% (95% CI, 79.6-82.2%) in 2017 (p < 0.001) (Figure 3A).

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: A commonly reported reason for not performing an EGFR mutation analysis was the lack of sufficient suitable tissue or a low percentage of tumor cells.

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: However, reasons for not performing an EGFR mutation analysis were not systematically captured in the pathology reports used in our study.

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: Therefore, it could not be determined with high confidence which other technical, patient or infrastructural factors contributed to not testing for EGFR mutations.

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: Samples from the patients in this study originated from 52 different pathology departments in the Netherlands.

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: Forty-one departments reported EGFR mutation test results for 10 or more patients in each of the three time periods (2013, 2015 and 2017).

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: The majority of departments improved their testing rates and the inter-pathology department variance in requesting EGFR testing gradually decreased from 2013 to 2017 (Figure S1).

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: In 2017, only four out of the 41 departments (9.8%) underperformed compared to the national average.

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: In other words, these departments reported fewer EGFR mutation tests (<60% of the eligible patients) than expected for their respective tumor volumes (based on the lower 99.7% CI limit) and the national average of 80.9% in 2017.

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: The landscape of tests used to detect EGFR mutations changed in the study years.

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: Whereas the most common tests in 2013 were high-resolution melting (HRM), mutation-specific polymerase chain reaction (PCR), single-gene sequencing (such as Sanger sequencing) or combinations thereof, EGFR testing was mostly performed (78.7%) with multi-gene assays in 2017 (Figure 3B).

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: The use of multi-gene assays as first-line molecular diagnostics surged from 7.8% in 2013 to 55.4% in 2015 (p < 0.001), and further increased to 78.7% in 2017 (p < 0.001) (Figure 3C).

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: Laboratories generally use custom or generic NGS panels validated in accordance with national accreditation guidelines (ISO-NEN-15189:2012 since 2016/2017).

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: Examples of more common NGS assays are custom AmpliSeq-panels on an IonTorrent platform [], the TruSeq Amplicon Cancer Panel-based NGS using a MiSeq Personal sequencer [], and the nationally aligned single-molecule Molecular Inversion Probe (smMIP) PATHv2D panel on an Illumina platform [].

body.section: 3.2. EGFR Testing Rates, Inter-Pathology Department Variance and Assays Used
body.text: The panels used by Dutch molecular pathology laboratories all covered the full region of interest in EGFR (exons 18-21).

body.section: 3.3. Landscape of EGFR Mutations in Untreated Dutch NSCLC Patients
body.text: Of the 7908 patients tested for EGFR mutations at initial diagnosis, one or more mutations were reported in 11.7% of all cases (95% CI, 11.0-12.4%; n = 925) (Table 2).

body.section: 3.3. Landscape of EGFR Mutations in Untreated Dutch NSCLC Patients
body.text: Female patients were more likely to harbor EGFR mutations (16.0%; 95% CI, 14.8-17.2%; n = 600) than male patients (7.8%; 95% CI, 7.0-8.6; n = 325; p < 0.001).

body.section: 3.3. Landscape of EGFR Mutations in Untreated Dutch NSCLC Patients
body.text: There were no significant differences in EGFR positivity between the three study years (Figure 3D) nor between the use of single-gene or multi-gene assays (Figure 3E).

body.section: 3.3. Landscape of EGFR Mutations in Untreated Dutch NSCLC Patients
body.text: The majority of patients harbored a classical, actionable exon 19 deletion (41% of 925 cases) or L858R (32%), whereas uncommon but actionable mutations (9%), exon 20 insertions (8%), and other not actionable/unknown variants (8%) constituted a much smaller proportion of the EGFR-mutant patients (Figure 3F).

body.section: 3.3. Landscape of EGFR Mutations in Untreated Dutch NSCLC Patients
body.text: On a variant class- or single mutant-level, no significant distribution differences were observed for the three study years (Figure 3G) nor for the use of single-gene or multi-gene assays (Figure 3H), except for EGFR L861X.

body.section: 3.3. Landscape of EGFR Mutations in Untreated Dutch NSCLC Patients
body.text: This variant (either alone or in combination with a second EGFR variant) was slightly more common in patients tested with a multi-gene assay (n = 20; 0.5% of those tested for EGFR mutations) compared to those tested with single-gene tests (n = 5; 0.2%; p = 0.036).

body.section: 3.4. Impact of EGFR Testing on First-Line Targeted Therapy and Subsequent Overall Survival
body.text: Treatment and survival data were available for 10,237 out of 10,254 patients (99.8%).

body.section: 3.4. Impact of EGFR Testing on First-Line Targeted Therapy and Subsequent Overall Survival
body.text: This included 390 patients with an exon 19 deletion, 287 patients with L858R, 103 patients with an uncommon, actionable variant, 69 patients with an exon 20 insertion, 61 patients with a not actionable/unknown variant and 6972 patients without EGFR mutation.

body.section: 3.4. Impact of EGFR Testing on First-Line Targeted Therapy and Subsequent Overall Survival
body.text: Patients who were not tested for EGFR mutations (n = 2343) were excluded from the analysis, as were patients reported to be EGFR mutation positive but for whom the exact variant was not reported (and could thus not be classified) (n = 12).

body.section: 3.4.1. Overall Survival of EGFR-Mutant Patients Versus Those without EGFR Mutations
body.text: OS in patients with any EGFR mutation was higher for those diagnosed in 2017 (median 18.1 months; 95% CI, 15.7-20.5) compared to 2013 (median 14.3 months; 95% CI, 12.5-16.1; p = 0.035), but similar to 2015 (median 17.6 months; 95% CI, 15.0-20.2; p = 0.988) (Figure 4A).

body.section: 3.4.1. Overall Survival of EGFR-Mutant Patients Versus Those without EGFR Mutations
body.text: Irrespective of first-line treatment, distinct survival patterns were observed in the different EGFR mutation subclasses (Figure 4B).

body.section: 3.4.1. Overall Survival of EGFR-Mutant Patients Versus Those without EGFR Mutations
body.text: Median OS in patients without EGFR mutations was 5.6 months (95% CI, 5.4-5.8) in the period 2013-2017.

body.section: 3.4.1. Overall Survival of EGFR-Mutant Patients Versus Those without EGFR Mutations
body.text: Evaluation of OS for the various EGFR mutation classes revealed a favorable OS for patients with exon 19 deletions (23.8 months; 95% CI, 20.8-26.7; p < 0.001), L858R (16.7 months; 95% CI, 14.1-19.3; p < 0.001) and uncommon, actionable variants (12.2 months; 95% CI, 9.4-15.0; p < 0.001).

body.section: 3.4.1. Overall Survival of EGFR-Mutant Patients Versus Those without EGFR Mutations
body.text: In contrast, median OS of patients with exon 20 insertions (11.1 months; 95% CI, 6.4-15.8; p = 0.071) or with not actionable/unknown variants (6.8 months; 95% CI, 4.3-9.4; p = 0.980) was comparable to the OS of patients without an EGFR mutation.

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: Out of the 910 patients with EGFR mutation(s) and available follow-up, 651 (72%) received first-line treatment with targeted therapy.

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: Of note, this included patients in the not actionable/unknown group (Tier III-IV), which today would likely not be treated with targeted therapy.

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: The proportion receiving targeted therapy was not affected by year of diagnosis (70%, 70% and 74% in 2013, 2015 and 2017, respectively; p = 0.332) (Figure S2).

body.text: There was no information on which inhibitor was used.

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: However, in 2013-2017, gefitinib, erlotinib and afatinib were the only EGFR inhibitors used in first-line therapy [].

body.text: The remaining patients (representing 29% of all EGFR-mutated patients) were either treated with a non-targeted modality (n = 171; 19%) or did not receive treatment (n = 88; 10%).

body.text: The NCR did not register reasons for not treating patients with targeted therapy, nor was this information available in the pathology reports.

body.text: Therefore, reasons for not treating patients with targeted therapy could not be investigated.

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: The proportion of patients receiving first-line targeted therapy was highest for those with an exon 19 deletion (321/390; 82%) or L858R mutation (227/287; 79%), lower for those with uncommon, actionable variants (69/103; 67%) and smallest for those with exon 20 insertions (18/69; 26%) and not actionable/unknown variants (16/61; 26%) (Figure 4C).

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: These proportions were not affected by year of diagnosis (Figure S2).

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: Distinct differences in survival were observed between the predefined categories of EGFR mutations (Figure 4D).

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: Median OS in patients treated with first-line targeted therapy was 26.4 months for patients with exon 19 deletions (95% CI, 23.5-29.2), 18.3 months for patients with L858R (95% CI, 15.7-21.0), 13.3 months for patients with uncommon, actionable variants (95% CI, 9.9-16.7), 6.7 months for patients with exon 20 insertions (95% CI, 0-13.4), and 7.1 months for patients with not actionable/unknown variants (95% CI, 6.4-7.8).

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: Uni- and multivariable Cox regression analyses were performed to evaluate whether the type of EGFR mutation is associated with OS (Table 3).

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: Because OS for patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions and patients with not actionable/unknown variants treated with first- and second-generation EGFR inhibitors was comparably poor (Figure 4D), these groups were pooled into one category dubbed as “resistant/unknown variants”.

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: A higher age (p < 0.001), male sex (p < 0.008) and diagnosis in 2013 (p = 0.011) were significantly associated with worse outcome in the univariate analyses.

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: When corrected for these factors, patients with EGFR exon 19 deletions showed superior outcomes compared to those with L858R (hazard ratio (HR) 1.6; 95% CI, 1.3-1.9; p < 0.001), uncommon, actionable variants (HR 2.1; 95% CI, 1.5-2.7; p < 0.001) and resistant/unknown variants (HR 4.7; 95% CI, 3.2-6.8; p < 0.001).

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: OS of patients with EGFR L858R when corrected for age, sex and year of diagnosis was not different from patients with uncommon actionable EGFR mutations (HR 1.31; 95% CI, 1.0-1.8; p = 0.069).

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: Furthermore, patients with resistant/unknown variants had a worse outcome compared to those with EGFR L858R (HR 3.0; 95% CI, 2.1-4.3; p < 0.001) or those with uncommon actionable variants (HR 2.4; 95% CI, 1.6-3.6; p < 0.001).

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: In 2017, the third-generation EGFR inhibitor osimertinib was approved for use in patients who developed the EGFR T790M mutation as a mechanism of resistance.

body.text: In this year, of the 254 patients who received an EGFR inhibitor, 27 (11%) developed the T790M within one year after diagnosis.

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: An additional 16 patients (6%) developed this mutation in the remainder of 2018.

body.text: The T790M mutation was detected on the background of an exon 19 deletion (27 out of 321 (8.4%) treated with targeted therapy), the L858R mutation (15/227; 6.6%) and the composite G719S/L861Q mutation (n = 1).

body.text: Because the reports were limited to 2018, the number of long-term responders cannot be estimated.

body.section: 3.4.2. Overall Survival in Patients Treated with First-Line Targeted Therapy
body.text: The NCR data did not contain information about the type of therapy in second-line nor the duration of response to second-line treatment.

body.text: Therefore, a survival analysis to investigate the impact of resistance-targeted treatment options could not be performed.

body.text: There is insufficient data to investigate whether the treatment-induced T790M is more prevalent on the background of an exon 19 deletion than L858R.

body.section: 4. Discussion
body.text: In this study, the impact of routine testing for EGFR mutations was investigated in the Dutch population of patients with newly diagnosed advanced ns-NSCLC in 2013, 2015 and 2017.

body.section: 4. Discussion
body.text: This analysis revealed that, despite a significant increase in testing rate and a nationwide shift from single-gene testing to multi-gene assays such as NGS, the EGFR positivity rate and distributions of specific (common and uncommon) alterations that can be observed at primary diagnosis remained comparable.

body.section: 4. Discussion
body.text: In addition, the analysis of real-world treatment outcome data in the Netherlands revealed distinct survival patterns for patients with different classes of EGFR mutations when treated in first-line with first- (gefitinib, erlotinib) or second-generation (afatinib) EGFR-TKI.

body.section: 4. Discussion
body.text: The results of this population-based analysis hold not only value for policy makers and healthcare providers, but also offer insight into the frequency and consequences of reported uncommon and composite variants for clinicians and scientists.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: Testing for EGFR mutations at primary diagnosis has been standard-of-care for advanced NSCLC patients in the Netherlands since 2011 [,].

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: Our analysis showed that the testing rate has since then gradually but significantly increased from 72.7% in 2013 to 80.2% in 2017 (p < 0.001).

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: Whether nationwide testing rates further increased thereafter will be the subject of future studies.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: Reasons for not performing an EGFR mutation analysis were not systematically captured in the pathology reports.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: The availability and suitability of sufficient tissue, patient factors negating the need for testing (death prior to testing, poor condition, or personal preference provided at shared decision-making visits) are likely important factors.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: However, it cannot be excluded that a percentage of eligible NSCLC patients are not offered predictive testing despite the availability of tissue and increasing number of registered (EGFR-)targeted therapies.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: The prevalence of EGFR mutations in the Dutch population of ns-NSCLC is 11.7% (95% CI, 11.0-12.4%).

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: This was comparable to the prevalence found in a smaller Dutch cohort in 2012 (10.6% in adenocarcinoma of the lung) [], though slightly lower than previously reported in a pooled prevalence analysis of studies with European subjects (14.1%) [].

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: As expected, EGFR mutations associated with EGFR inhibitor-induced on-target resistance mutations were not observed in this untreated cohort, except for one case.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: This single case of EGFR T790M without another mutation might suggests a germline event, but cannot be concluded without additional testing.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: The uptake of NGS as the method of choice for EGFR analysis (from 8% in 2013 to 79% in 2017) did not impact the nationwide detection rate of EGFR mutations nor the distribution of uncommon mutations.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: This is likely because the majority of single-gene tests in this study were sequencing techniques (such as pyrosequencing, Sanger sequencing or HRM in combination with sequencing) that covered the full region of interest in EGFR (exons 18-21).

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: The only variant impacted by the shift to multi-gene testing was the uncommon EGFR L861X mutation in exon 21.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: This variant was slightly more common in patients tested with a multi-gene assay compared to single-gene tests (p = 0.036).

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: The first reports on the actionability of this variant with first-generation EGFR-TKI emerged in 2018 [].

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: It is conceivable that this continuously increasing knowledge resulted in a more frequent reporting of previously unrecognized uncommon yet actionable EGFR variants.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: In addition, single-gene tests available in 2013-such as cobas® EGFR Mutation Test v1 (Roche Holding AG, Basel, Switzerland)-might not have been designed to capture an L861X mutation due to its previously unknown clinical significance.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: As such, the introduction of EGFR mutation analysis by NGS likely contributed to the discovery of treatment options for the current uncommon EGFR mutations.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: Our results indicate that the utilization of NGS did not adversely impact the detection rate for EGFR mutations underscoring the accurate detection of mutations.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: Median OS in the Dutch population of advanced ns-NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations was 18.1 months in 2017, which is comparable to other real-world studies with European subjects [].

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: Although median OS in patients diagnosed in 2015 was comparable (17.6 months), patients diagnosed in 2013 survived shorter (14.3 months, p = 0.035).

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: This may be because patients diagnosed in 2013 generally did not have access to second-line testing and novel treatment options.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: For example, a multitude of potential resistance mechanisms to first- and second-generation EGFR-TKIs therapies have been reported, most commonly the T790M resistance mutation [].

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: The activity of third-generation inhibitors, such as osimertinib, in first and later lines of therapy, is unaffected by this mutation [].

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: In addition, checkpoint inhibition has been approved for patients with tumors expressing PD-L1.

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: This has improved survival rates in advanced NSCLC patients [].

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: Checkpoint inhibitors are not used in first- or second-line treatment of EGFR-mutant patients as they do not improve OS in these patients [].

body.section: 4.1. Impact of Routine EGFR Testings on Detection of EGFR Mutations and Overall Survival
body.text: Unfortunately, assessment of the impact of the introduction of the new treatment modalities could not be performed as the NCR database lacks information on second and later lines of treatment.

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: The number of options for targeted therapy for NSCLC patients beyond EGFR has strongly increased.

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Different therapies are now registered or being tested in trials for patients with an activating mutation ALK [], BRAF [], ERBB2 [], MET [], NTRK1-3 [], RET [], and ROS1 [].

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: In addition, trials with specific KRAS G12C inhibitors demonstrate strong clinical benefit with registration expected by the end of 2021 [].

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: As such, the panel of therapeutically relevant biomarkers in NSCLC is continuously increasing.

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Testing patients for all these predictive markers using consecutive single-gene tests is inefficient considering the often limited amount of available tissue.

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Therefore, NGS has become standard-of-care in the Netherlands to simultaneously test for all relevant actionable mutations also beyond EGFR as an efficient diagnostic work-up [].

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Although the content of the panels has changed since 2017, the current core set of genes relevant for NSCLC was already analyzed in 2017.

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Due to higher volumes of NGS tests, the turnaround times and costs per sample have decreased.

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Improvements of library preparation methods and optimization of sample procurement has decreased the number of samples that could not be analyzed due to low tissue volume.

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Publicly available cohort databases such as the AACR project GENIE database indicate that EGFR-activating mutations are mutually exclusive with other known driver mutations [].

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: However, co-occurrence of mutations in other genes may affect survival and response to EGFR-TKI [].

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Notably, the prognostic value of TP53 mutations in combination has been demonstrated [].

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Patients with concurrent EGFR and TP53 mutations may benefit from combining EGFR-TKI with anti-VEGF therapies such as bevacizumab [], ramucirumab [], or apatinib [].

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: Because TP53 was not part of the list of genes that must be sequenced in the context of NSCLC in the Netherlands in the study period [], most laboratories did not report mutations in these genes.

body.section: 4.2. Beyond EGFR
body.text: As such, our results could not be stratified for co-occurrence of EGFR and TP53 mutations.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: Previous reports on nationwide real-world data regarding the effect of EGFR mutation status and response to EGFR inhibitors generally lack detailed information with respect to EGFR mutation type [,,,,].

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: In smaller cohorts, EGFR mutation status and response rates have been reported, but irrespective of evidence of response to first- and second-generation EGFR-TKI, often including T790M resistance mutations, exon 20 insertions and variants of unknown significance [,,,,,].

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: Furthermore, the EGFR L858R mutation and exon 19 deletions are often pooled together as ‘common’ mutations [,], due to their frequency but despite a difference in response in the Asian population [].

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: In a recent, unpublished study, Robichaux et al. suggested four subgroups: classical-like, T790M-like, exon 20 insertions and ATP binding-pocket volume-reducing (PVR) mutations [].

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: However, also in this study exon 19 deletions and L858R were pooled into the classical-like group, and included combinations between a common and an uncommon mutation in the ‘PVR’ group.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: In contrast, it may be more appropriate to classify variants based on their respective sensitivity to individual inhibitors in terms of survival [].

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: Thus, we differentiated EGFR variants in terms of frequency and actionability with first- and second-generation EGFR-TKI.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: The classification scheme proposed by the 2017 AMP/ASCO/CAP guidelines [], was used to individually classify all detected variants into EGFR “exon 19 deletion” (Tier I), “L858R” (Tier I) and into three groups of uncommon variants: “exon 20 insertions” (Tier II), “uncommon, actionable variants” including known double mutations such as S768I/L861Q and G719A/S768I (Tier I or II) and “not actionable/unknown variants” (Tier III or IV) (Figure 1 and Table 4).

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: This classification scheme revealed distinct survival characteristics in patients treated with first-line targeted therapy.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: Patients with an EGFR exon 19 deletion, L858R or uncommon actionable mutation benefit from first- and second-generation EGFR inhibitors, albeit to a different extent (median OS 95% CI: 20.8-26.7, 14.1-19.3, 9.4-15.1 months, respectively).

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: OS for patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions and not actionable/unknown variants was comparable to patients without an EGFR mutation who were not treated with an inhibitor.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: The current study confirmed the superior OS for patients with an EGFR exon 19 deletions compared the L858R mutation (adjusted HR of L858R versus exon 19 deletion was 1.57; p < 0.001) [].

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: When corrected for covariates such as age, sex and year of diagnosis, the difference in OS for patients with an EGFR L858R or uncommon actionable mutation was not significant (HR uncommon, EGFR actionable variants versus L858R: 1.311; p = 0.069).

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: It should be noted that the majority of these patients were treated with first-generation EGFR-TKIs gefitinib or erlotinib [], which may be less effective in patients with uncommon EGFR mutations than afatinib [,], or osimertinib [].

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: Afatinib was likely used in a minority of patients [], and osimertinib was not available for first-line treatment in the study period.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: Thus, survival rates for L858R and uncommon, actionable variants may be even more similar with newer agents but has to be investigated.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: Collectively, these results reinforce the notion that future clinical trials need to avoid pooling EGFR L858R and exon 19 deletions into a single category, and warrants further investigation into the similarities between L858R and ‘uncommon, actionable’ variants.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: Both patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions and patients with variants classified as ‘not actionable/unknown’ showed dismal survival when treated with first- or second-generation EGFR-TKI in first-line.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: Both categories were considered as ‘resistant’ to first- and second-generation EGFR-TKI: the former category because these are known to be non-responsive to first- and second-generation TKI [], and the latter because (pre)clinical evidence on actionability is lacking.

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: However, these perspectives might change with new evidence: for example, there are promising novel agents and combination therapies currently under investigation that may be effective against EGFR exon 20 insertions, including amivantamab [], poziotinib [], and mobocertinib [], or combining osimertinib or afatinib with cetuximab [].

body.section: 4.3. A Clinical Evidence-Driven Reclassification of EGFR Mutations
body.text: In the Netherlands, all Tier II and III EGFR variants are nowadays commonly discussed in Molecular Tumor Boards [], resulting in favorable treatment outcomes [].

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: Although the PALGA registry offers nationwide coverage on pathology testing in the Netherlands, the collected information in the study period represented narrative pathology reports in routine diagnostics.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: Thus, if patients were tested for EGFR mutations for research purposes or if the pathologist in charge did not include testing results in the pathology report, patients may have been missed and the testing rate may be underestimated.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: Similarly, the NCR, which also has nationwide coverage and therefore allows for unique real-world analyses, has several limitations.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: First, it does not include treatment-specific information such as best overall response or progression-free survival and is limited to first-line treatment.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: Second, the NCR did not register reasons for not treating patients with targeted therapy; thus, we could not investigate why circa 20% of patients with common EGFR mutations were not treated with EGFR-targeted therapy.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: Finally, information on which EGFR-TKI was specifically used for each patient was not provided, but was restricted to first- (gefitinib, erlotinib) and second-generation (afatinib) inhibitors that could have been used in the period 2013-2017.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: In 2017, osimertinib became available which has made a positive impact on overall survival.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: Due to the limitations of the NCR database, this impact could not be quantified.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: The clinical impact of currently available third-generation inhibitors on EGFR variants in second-line testing and multiple lines of treatment was therefore not the subject of this study.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: Despite the increase in the use of NGS, the current study did not capture mutations in genes other than EGFR.

body.section: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
body.text: As such, frequencies of other driver mutations are not reported and a complete landscape of mutations in the known drivers is not presented.

body.section: 5. Conclusions
body.text: In the period 2013-2017, EGFR mutation testing in the Netherlands has transformed from a single-gene approach to the nationwide implementation of NGS using a multigene panel for predictive biomarker testing including EGFR according to the current Dutch national guideline for lung cancer [].

body.section: 5. Conclusions
body.text: This shift did not affect the overall detection rate of EGFR mutations (11.7%) nor the distribution of mutations.

body.section: 5. Conclusions
body.text: In patients treated with first-line targeted therapy, EGFR exon 19 deletions, L858R, and uncommon, actionable variants were all independently associated with improved survival compared to patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions or not actionable/unknown variants.

body.section: 5. Conclusions
body.text: Furthermore, we demonstrated that overall survival in patients with L858R is more comparable to those with uncommon, actionable mutations than to those with EGFR exon 19 deletions.

body.section: 5. Conclusions
body.text: These results indicate that distinguishing between EGFR exon 19 deletions and L858R mutations, as well as classifying actionability of uncommon variants using the 2017 AMP/ASCO/CAP guidelines, is a more appropriate method to predict actionability and survival than the grouping of mutations into ‘common’ and ‘uncommon’ variants based on their frequencies in the patient population.
